extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, hearing decision-makers, and other recipients required to implement §106.45 grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance for administering §106.45 Title IX grievance processes at postsecondary institutions, focusing on evidentiary rules, live-hearing procedures, rape-shield protections, decision-maker duties, and related procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-reliance on statements not submitted to cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision-maker must not rely on the statement of a party or witness who does not submit to cross-examination; this exclusion covers statements (oral or written) made by a person who refuses or fails to submit to cross-examination, even if those statements might be admissible under civil or criminal evidentiary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: cross-examination serves a unique credibility-testing, truth-seeking function that non-courtroom Title IX proceedings lack the evidentiary framework to replicate. This exclusion may lead to more reliable outcomes than permitting reliance on untested statements. It applies to allegations in a formal complaint if the complainant does not appear or refuses to be cross-examined. Recipients should still afford parties and witnesses opportunities (including remote testimony) to appear and be cross-examined. The prohibition on reliance includes statements contained in police reports, SANE reports, medical reports, and other documents to the extent they contain a person's statements of someone who did not submit to cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'submit to cross-examination' (answer relevant questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'submit to cross-examination' means answering cross-examination questions that are determined to be relevant by the decision-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers must make relevance determinations in real time during the hearing to protect parties from irrelevant questioning. If a party/witness refuses to answer a question deemed relevant by the decision-maker, their statements may be excluded unless the decision-maker reconsiders relevance before reaching the determination regarding responsibility. The party's reason for refusing does not matter for exclusion. Appearing but not engaging in the cross-examination procedure does not count as 'submitting.'

rubrics_metrics.name: No inference from non-appearance or refusal to be cross-examined
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers must not draw any inference regarding responsibility based solely on a party's or witness's absence from the hearing or refusal to be cross-examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects parties (including respondents asserting Fifth Amendment concerns) from adverse presumptions due to non-appearance or refusal to submit to cross-examination. Where a respondent fails to appear, the decision-maker may still consider relevant evidence (excluding statements of the non-appearing party) and reach a determination, but the final regulations do not characterize this as a 'default judgment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Only relevant evidence may be relied upon by decision-maker
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers must objectively evaluate and rely only on evidence that is 'relevant' to the allegations when reaching determinations regarding responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigatory process may gather broader evidence, but investigators should summarize only relevant evidence in the investigative report. Decision-makers retain discretion to assign weight and credibility to relevant evidence, but relevance is the sole admissibility/exclusion criterion (rather than balancing probative value against unfair prejudice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape shield protections (sexual history and predisposition rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions or evidence about a complainant's sexual predisposition are always irrelevant; questions or evidence about a complainant's prior sexual behavior are irrelevant except in two limited exceptions: (1) offered to prove someone other than the respondent committed the alleged offense, or (2) where prior sexual behavior is specifically about the complainant and the respondent and is offered to prove consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adapted language from Fed. R. Evid. 412 but did not import its balancing test. Decision-makers must treat sexual predisposition as categorically irrelevant with no exceptions; prior sexual behavior is irrelevant unless it fits one of the two concrete exceptions. The rape shield protections apply at hearings and are deemed to render such questions/evidence irrelevant. The protections are focused on complainants and are not extended as a special rule to respondents, though in counter-claim situations a party designated as a 'complainant' must be protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-makers must be trained on relevance and rape shield application
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must train decision-makers on issues of relevance, including specific application of rape shield protections and how to determine relevance in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training may include information about the Advisory Committee Note to Fed. R. Evid. 412 so long as it remains focused on applying the rape shield protections as formulated in these regulations. The Department expects recipients to ensure correct application despite studies that lawyers sometimes circumvent rape shield protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on coercing victims to participate
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is prohibited from coercing unwilling victims to participate in a grievance process, even when investigating serial predators or serious allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must offer supportive measures (e.g., no-contact orders) and may not compel victims to participate; recipients can use alternative measures like emergency removals and supportive measures to address safety concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures and non-punitive accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must offer supportive measures to complainants (and may offer to respondents) such as forbidding contact or communication, separate-room hearings, advisors of choice, virtual appearance options, and rules of decorum to reduce trauma and inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must grant requests to hold live hearings with parties in separate rooms; questioning may not be conducted by the respondent personally. Recipients may allow virtual participation provided technology permits simultaneous seeing and hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology requirement for virtual live hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: If recipients permit participants to appear virtually for a live hearing, technology must enable all participants to simultaneously see and hear each other; telephonic-only participation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the integrity of the hearing and supports cross-examination functionality for remote witnesses/parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative report must summarize only relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although investigators may gather a broad universe of evidence during investigation, the investigative report must summarize only evidence that is relevant to the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may review all evidence 'directly related to the allegations' during investigation, but the investigative report should exclude information deemed not relevant (including sexual-history information excluded by rape-shield protections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment records and legal privilege protections
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's treatment records cannot be used without the party's voluntary, written consent, and information protected by a legally recognized privilege cannot be used in the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections operate alongside the exclusion of untested statements and rape-shield protections to safeguard privacy and privileged communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients lack subpoena power; cannot compel testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients and parties generally lack subpoena power to compel witnesses to appear and testify; institutions should not be converted into de facto courtrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should thoughtfully work with witnesses on scheduling and use discretion to permit remote testimony to reduce absences; where witnesses cannot or will not appear and be cross-examined, their statements cannot be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity and recipient obligation to gather and present evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties and the recipient have equal opportunities (and, for the recipient, the obligation) to gather and present relevant evidence, including fact and expert witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both sides face the same limitations due to lack of subpoena power. The recipient must ensure procedures allow fair opportunity to present evidence while maintaining the exclusion rules (e.g., non-reliance on untested statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker may consider evidence excluding untested statements when party absent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party (e.g., a complainant) fails to appear for a hearing, a decision-maker may still consider relevant evidence—excluding that party's statements—and reach a determination regarding responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipient discretion under §106.45(b)(3)(ii) allows dismissal in some circumstances (withdrawal, respondent no longer enrolled/employed, or inability to gather sufficient evidence). The process should not infer responsibility from absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of evidence must apply consistently and not be tied to reliance on untested statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may choose between available standards of evidence but must apply the chosen standard to all formal complaints processed under §106.45; reliance on statements not subject to cross-examination must not be tied to or vary by the chosen standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making admissibility or reliance on untested statements dependent on the standard would undermine predictability and recipient discretion. Changes in the final regulations clarify that a recipient's choice of standard applies to all formal complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: No waiver of cross-examination to circumvent exclusion rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations decline to permit parties or witnesses to 'waive' cross-examination questions in a way that would circumvent the exclusion of untested statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing waivers would defeat the truth-seeking purposes of cross-examination in the Title IX context; appearing but refusing to engage does not count as submitting to cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination distinct from decision-maker questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-examination (adversarial questioning by the parties/advisors) is distinct from neutral questions posed by the decision-maker; only cross-examination constitutes the unique credibility-testing opportunity whose absence triggers exclusion of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party's refusal to answer a decision-maker's questions does not preclude the decision-maker from relying on that party's statements, because those questions do not replace adversarial cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may remove respondent on emergency basis without cross-examination during removal challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations allow recipients to remove a respondent on an emergency (immediate threat) basis and do not require cross-examination during the post-removal opportunity to challenge the removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency removals and supportive measures are distinct safety-preserving tools and do not implicate the cross-examination reliance rule for live hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on retaliation for participating or refusing to participate
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.71 prohibits retaliation against any person exercising rights under Title IX, including participating or refusing to participate in any grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection applies equally to those who choose not to appear or to refuse cross-examination and ensures no adverse actions for exercising Title IX rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of what counts as a 'statement' for exclusion purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Statements' have their ordinary meaning and include a person's intent to make factual assertions; they do not include evidence that does not constitute a person's factual assertion (e.g., videos without statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents containing statements (police reports, medical records) may not be relied on to the extent they contain the statements of a party/witness who did not submit to cross-examination; probing credibility of statements contained in such documents requires the opportunity to cross-examine the person who made them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-makers need not possess judge-level legal expertise; keep procedures administrable
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations avoid importing complex evidentiary balancing tests (e.g., probative value vs unfair prejudice) because non-lawyer decision-makers at educational institutions should not be expected to apply comprehensive rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using relevance as the single admissibility test and the concrete rape-shield exceptions seeks to ensure lay decision-makers can competently implement the rules without turning institutions into courts.
